newsitem.title: SWITZERLAND: BIS says will open records to Nazi gold inquiries.
newsitem.headline: BIS says will open records to Nazi gold inquiries.

text.p: The Bank for International Settlements (BIS) said it would cooperate with any competent authority -- such as a Berne-appointed commission of experts or Holocaust account panel -- that wished to examine its records with regards to the fate of Nazi gold.
"We would cooperate with competent authorities when requests are made," BIS general secretary Gunter Baer told Reuters in response to inquiries.

Basle-based BIS, central bank to the worlds' central banks, has been drawn into the current debate over the fate of Nazi gold because of its role in overseeing reparations from Germany to the Allied governments following World War One.
U.S. senator Alfonse D'Amato, chairman of the Senate banking committee, recently wrote to BIS general manager Andrew Crockett, asking BIS to publish its records covering Nazi gold.
Under the 1930 Hague Agreement and the Young Plan, which established the BIS as an instititution, Germany's Reichsbank paid BIS interest payments in the form of gold.

Following World War Two and the Paris Reparation Agreement in 1946, BIS then handed back to the Allied Powers 3.7 tonnes of gold, which had been identified as looted gold and had been paid to BIS by the Reichsbank.
The Swiss government on Monday endorsed an official inquiry into the whereabouts of both Nazi and Jewish wealth held by Swiss banks during World War Two.
The issue of Nazi theft of Jewish citizen's assets and the transfer of assets owned by Holocast victims to Switzerland was raised by a British government report issued last week.
The government gave its backing to a bill in the works since May that would create a commission of experts empowered to lift Swiss bank secrecy laws.
Former U.S. Federal Reserve Board Chairman Paul Volcker also heads a panel of experts from the Swiss Banker's Association and world Jewish groups to look for lost Holocaust accounts.
As an international institution, BIS is not subject to Swiss banking secrecy acts so opening its records would purely be to show that it is willing to cooperate, Baer said.
BIS, however, is owned by central banks and only provides services to central banks. Private persons cannot conduct banking business with BIS.
Separately from the issue of Nazi gold, BIS has been organising and sorting its records dating back to its founding in 1930 over the last 18 months.
Baer said the issue of whether these records could be opened to historians was a matter for the board, which is made up of central bank governors from the Group of 10 (G10) rich nations.

While opening records is a sensitive issue for any bank -- due to client confidentiality -- the issue is even more sensitive to BIS because of the confidential character of the central bank meetings held at the BIS.
